abstract.p: The RIG-I-like receptors (RLRs) assemble into filamentous structures that initiate type-I interferon (IFN-I) and NF-κB signaling pathways via the adaptor protein MAVS and subsequent downstream signaling cascades. The formation and regulation of these filaments are influenced by numerous cellular proteins and complexes. In this study, we identified the stress-responsive heat shock protein HSPA6, which is induced upon RLR activation and acts as a negative regulator of IFN-I signaling. The expression of HSPA6 is independent of MAVS or IRF3 but is dependent on the E3 ligases associated with RLRs, stress granules (SGs), and the transcription factors IRF1 and AP-1. HSPA6 downregulates RLR-mediated IFN signaling by binding to these receptors in the cytoplasm and disrupting the formation of multimer complexes. Collectively, our findings reveal a novel feedback mechanism by RLRs that is distinct from the canonical IRF3-dependent IFN-I activation or NF-κB-mediated inflammatory cytokine induction.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The type I interferon (IFN-I) signaling pathway plays a pivotal role in the defense against pathogen invasions. Pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) sense pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) or damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) to activate IFN-I expression. In the cytoplasm, virus-derived double-stranded RNAs (dsRNAs) are recognized by MDA5 (melanoma differentiation-associated gene 5) or RIG-I (retinoic acid-inducible gene I). Alongside LGP2 (laboratory of genetics and physiology 2), these PRRs are collectively referred to as RIG-I-like receptors (RLRs). RIG-I specifically binds to the 5’-ppp or 5’-pp ends of short dsRNA molecules and hydrolyzes ATP to translocate into the RNA interior [1]. MDA5 prefers long dsRNA and binds internally within the RNA molecule, with additional MDA5 molecules quickly recruited to form a filament [2]. Both receptors utilize ATP hydrolysis to dynamically verify the authenticity of their RNA substrates [3]. The RLR filament interacts with MAVS (mitochondrial antiviral signaling protein) through CARDRLR-CARDMAVS (caspase activation and recruitment domain) interactions, leading to the aggregation of MAVS, which in turn, serves as a platform for the activation of downstream kinases and transcription factors such as TBK1 (TANK binding kinase 1), IRF3 (interferon regulatory factor 3), and NF-kB (nuclear factor kappa B) to activate IFN-I and NF-kB signaling. LGP2, lacking a CARD domain to bind to MAVS, is considered a regulatory protein that modulates the activity of RIG-I and MDA5 [4].

The regulatory machinery can be constitutively expressed or induced by IFN-I. PRR genes like IFIH1 (encoding MDA5) and DDX58 (encoding RIG-I) are inducible by IFN-I. This positive feedback loops enhances the cellular sensitivity to incoming infections, but it also risks misidentifying endogenous dsRNA elements, like those from retrotransposons. Cells employ various strategies to prevent this misidentifying, including the expression of constitutive ADAR1p110 (RNA-specific adenosine deaminase 1) and the IFN-inducible ADAR1p150. These enzymes bind to dsRNA and perform A-to-I editing, converting A: U base pairs to I: U mismatch, which disrupts the structure of endogenous dsRNA elements [5]. Recent research has underscored the importance of a group of E3 ubiquitin (Ub) ligases in the formation of RLR filaments. TRIM65 (tripartite motif containing 65) and RIPLET are essential for MDA5- and RIG-I-mediated IFN activation, respectively. These ligases selectively target filaments for ubiquitination [6, 7].

To investigate the regulation of IFN-I signaling, synthetic dsRNA such as poly I: C is extensively utilized. This dsRNA activates RLRs in a manner akin to natural viral dsRNA, yet it is not complicated by viral proteins that could adversely affect cellular conditions and IFN-I signaling activation. However, dsRNA triggers not only IFN-I transcription via RLRs but also a global shutdown of translation and RNA degradation through interactions with PKR (protein kinase R) and OASes (oligoadenylate synthases), respectively [8]. This makes it challenging to isolate the feedback regulation of IFN-I signaling. Conversely, the GOF (gain-of-function) mutant of RLRs can recognize the naturally occurring endogenous RNAs and induce IFN-I transcription [9]. As such, GOF mutants offer a valuable tool for studying the feedback mechanisms of IFN signaling without significantly disrupting the cellular environment.

Here, we discovered that HSPA6, a stress-induced member of the heat shock protein (HSP) family, is upregulated by interferon-competent RLRs. Interestingly, HSPA6 was not an interferon-stimulated gene (ISG), and its upregulation occurs independently of IRF3 or NF-κB. Functional assays involving overexpression (OE) and gene knockout (KO) revealed HSPA6’s negative regulatory role in IFN-I activation. Mechanistic studies suggested that HSPA6 interacts with MDA5, reducing the levels of multimeric proteins. These findings uncovered a new feedback axis mediated by RLR activation-induced stress that has never been identified, and raise the interesting question of whether other multimeric events in response to stimuli can regulate gene expression beyond the canonical cascades.

sec.title: HSPA6 is upregulated in expression during MDA5-mediated IFN signaling activation
sec.p: To avoid global RNA degradation induced by overwhelmingly introduced dsRNAs, we used GOF MDA5(G495R), an IFN-competent mutant whose activity relies on endogenous IR-Alu elements [10]. Protein expression was validated by Western blotting, and the cell viability was not impacted (Fig. S1A-S1F). We performed an RNA-seq to compare gene expression in WT and GOF MDA5 expressing cells (Fig. 1A). Data showed that most up-regulated genes in GOF MDA5 expressing cells were ISGs (Fig. S1G), consistent with previous observations [10, 11]. Among the rest of the changed genes, we found HSPA6 was upregulated in both RNA and protein levels by GOF mutant but not WT MDA5 (Fig. 1B). We also noticed that the basal expression level of HSPA6 was very low, in line with the notion that this chaperon protein is stress-induced and barely expressed at homeostasis status [12]. Other family members such as HSPA4 and HSPA12A were not affected in the sequencing data (Fig. S1H). Consistently, IFNβ treatment did not stimulate HSPA6 transcription (Fig. 1C). The HSPA6 gene is buried in the intron region of a large sequence named AL590385.23. Detection of the nearby sequences showed no changes upon GOF MDA5 expression (Fig. 1D), suggesting HSPA6 was induced independent on AL590385.23. No Alu elements or other retroelements could be found on this gene through UCSC Genome Browser searching [13].

sec.p: Next, we stimulated WT MDA5 with high molecular weight (HMW) poly I: C dsRNA. An increase in HSPA6 RNA level was observed in HEK293T cells (Fig. 1E) and HeLa cells (Fig. S1I). The observation that poly I: C alone stimulated HSPA6 expression in HeLa cells but not in HEK293T cells could be explained by the different basal expression levels of MDA5 in these two cell lines [14]. Thus, we concluded that IFN-competent MDA5 stimulates HSPA6 expression.

We further compared the kinetics of IFNβ and HSPA6 expression. Data showed that IFNβ reached its peak quickly and then dropped, while HSPA6 induction was slower but more steadily (Fig. 1F). Given that HSPA6 is not an ISG, this delayed stimulation suggested that it is mediated through a different manner from the TBK1-IRF3 axis or the IFNAR1-JAK-STAT axis. We treated GOF MDA5 expressing cells with actinomycin D (Act.D) to block global transcription and found that both IFNβ and HSPA6 RNA were significantly impacted upon drug treatment (Fig. 1G and H). Given that the basal level of HSPA6 was very low in previous tests, we concluded that this elimination by Act.D is due to the loss of transcription. Moreover, the dynamic of RNA abundance between 24 and 48 h was consistent with the results shown in Fig. 1F. Taken together, our data indicated that HSPA6 is transcriptionally upregulated in the process of MDA5 activating IFN signaling.

We next validated HSPA6 upregulation using encephalomyocarditis virus (EMCV) which is targeted by MDA5 [15]. Both IFNβ and HSPA6 levels were upregulated 24 h post-infection (Fig. 1I and J). The GEO database study also revealed that in other MDA5-targeting virus infections, an increase in HSPA6 expression was observed (accession GSE17400) (Fig. 1K) [16].

sec.title: RLR activates HSPA6 expression independently on MAVS
sec.p: MDA5 and RIG-I share structural similarities, functional commonalities, and use the same adaptor protein MAVS to trigger the downstream events. We set to investigate if RIG-I also stimulates HSPA6 expression. We used a GOF form of RIG-I (C268F) [17] that activates IFNβ transcription independent of exogenous dsRNA (Fig. S2A). Similar to MDA5, GOF RIG-I enhanced HSPA6 expression while WT RIG-I did not (Fig. 2A). In line with these, RIG-I-sensed Sendai virus (SeV) [15] stimulated HSPA6 expression upon infection (Fig. 2B). The GEO database searching for RIG-I-sensed viruses (accession GSE202409 and GSE130005) [18, 19] also supported our findings (Fig. 2C). In contrast, the cGAS-STING axis does not affect HSPA6 expression (Fig. 2D), but DNA virus HSV-1 infection also led to strong IFNβ and HSPA6 upregulation (Fig. S2B, C). Given the complexity of HSV-1 infection [20], we speculated that HSPA6 is upregulated by other mechanisms here.

sec.p: Next, we asked if MDA5 and RIG-I activate HSPA6 expression in a MAVS-dependent manner. We generated MAVS-KO cells (Fig. 2E) to find that GOF MDA5 no longer activates IFN-I signaling (Fig. 2F). However, HSPA6 upregulation was not affected (Fig. 2G). The NF-κB induced CCL5 was upregulated by GOF MDA5 based on RNA-seq data (Fig. S1A) and its expression was also dependent on MAVS (Fig. 2H), consistent with previous findings [21]. Notably, IRF3-KO (Fig. 2I) blocked IFNβ expression (Fig. 2J) but enhanced HSPA6 expression (Fig. 2K). We hypothesized that HSPA6 and IFNβ induction share common factors, and in the absence of IRF3, the transcription of HSPA6 is favored. Taken together, our data implicated that HSPA6 is upregulated through a parallel stress-related response rather than the classical IFN signaling pathway (Fig. 2L).

sec.title: E3 Ub ligases are required for HSPA6 upregulation
sec.p: The filamentous form of MDA5 is associated with TRIM65, which orchestrates the ubiquitination of MDA5 at Lys743, a critical step for the activation of IFN signaling [6, 14]. Similarly, RIG-I filament binds to a TRIM-like protein RIPLET [22] (Fig. 3A). We thus asked if these E3 Ub ligases are required for HSPA6 upregulation. We generated TRIM65-KO cells (Fig. S3A) and indeed observed the IFN-I induction by MDA5 disappeared (Fig. 3B). Concurrently, the expression of HSPA6 was also not induced (Fig. 3C). The R705A or K743E of MDA5 was shown to block TRIM65 binding, while K743R inhibited TRIM65-mediated MDA5 ubiquitination [6, 14]. We observed that these mutants on GOF MDA5 abolished HSPA6 upregulation (Fig. 3D and E). The expression of mutants was validated by western blotting (Fig. S3B) and their inability to induce IFNβ expression was validated by RT-qPCR (Fig. S3C, D). Similarly, in RIPLET-KO cells (Fig. S3E), neither IFNβ nor HSPA6 was induced in expression upon RIG-I activation (Fig. S3F, G). Taken together, our observation indicated that E3 Ub ligases targeting RLR filaments play essential roles in activating not only IFNβ induction but also HSPA6 expression.

sec.title: Stress granule is required for HSPA6 upregulation
sec.p: A bulk of evidence suggested that stress granules (SGs) are closely linked to filamentous RLRs and MAVS upon dsRNA treatment [23–26]. This led us to hypothesize that SG may serve as a hub to transmit downstream signals to activate not only IFNβ transcription but also HSPA6 transcription. As HSPA6 was hardly induced at early timepoints post stimulation, we tested whether SGs are required from 24 h post transfection (hpt). G3BP1 and G3BP2 proteins are required for SG formation [26]. We first treated cells with EGCG, a chemical that interferes with G3BP1 and blocks SG activity [27]. Data showed that at 24 hpt, both IFNβ and HSPA6 RNA levels were decreased upon EGCG treatment (Fig. 3F and G), suggesting SG is required for HSPA6 upregulation. Next, we established G3BP1/2-KO cells (Fig. S3H) and confirmed that SGs are required for both IFN-I signaling (Fig. S3I) and HSPA6 stimulation (Fig. 3H), in line with the previous observations. The poly I: C-stimulated WT MDA5 also relied on SGs for optimal IFN signaling activation (Fig. S3J) and HSPA6 transcription stimulation (Fig. 3I). The requirement of SG in mediated RIG-I-induced IFN (Fig. S3K) and HSPA6 expression (Fig. 3J) were also observed. To sum up, both E3 Ub ligases and SG are required for RLR activating HSAP6 transcription (Fig. 3K).

sec.title: AP1 and IRF1 are transcription factors essential for HSPA6 induction
sec.p: HSPA6 was reported to be transcribed by heat shock transcription factor 1 (HSF1) in stressed conditions [28, 29]. HSF1 localizes in the cytoplasm bound to the HSP40-HSP70-HSP90 complex as an inactive form. Upon stress stimulation, the HSPs turn to bind misfolded proteins, which in turn, causes HSF1 to translocate into the nucleus and activate gene transcription, including HSPA6 (Fig. 4A, upper panel) [28]. We knocked out HSP40 (DNAJB1) (Fig. S4A) to release HSF1 (Fig. 4A, lower panel) [30] and found that HSPA6 RNA level was upregulated in HSP40-KO cells (Fig. 4B). Given that HSP40 was reported to disrupt MDA5 filament formation [31], we deduced HSPA6 upregulation in HSP40-KO cells could result from combining effects by raising more MDA5 filaments, as well as the release of HSF1. To further clarify the role of HSF1, we generated HSF1-KO cells (Fig. S4B) and found that HSPA6 upregulation was impaired in the KO cells (Fig. 4C).

sec.p: Due to the transcription activation was still evident in HSF1-KO cells, we asked if other transcription factors were required. We first tested HSPA4, HSPA12A, and DNAJA1 RNA levels by RT-qPCR. In line with our previous data (Fig. S1B), these HSPs were not upregulated upon GOF MDA5 expression (Fig. 4D-F). We hypothesized that the transcription factors for HSPA6 induction would not be those responsible for these unchanged HSPs (namely, other HSPs) (Fig. 4G). Then, we set a 2 kb long upstream of the mRNA as the promoter region and used a virtual laboratory PROMO to predict transcription factors [32, 33]. Three transcription factors were predicted not shared by other HSPs (Fig. 4H). We generated KO cells for IRF1 (Fig. S4C), AP1 (sgRNA targeting c-Jun) (Fig. S4D), and RXRalpha (Fig. S4E). In line with previous report [34, 35], IRF1 and AP1 were required for IFNβ induction (Fig. 4I). Strikingly, they were also required for HSPA6 transcription (Fig. 4J). Genomic searching in the 2 kb promoter region identified several putative binding sequences (AP1: 5’-TGAGTGA-3’; IRF1: 5’-GAAA…GAAA-3’) for both transcription factors (Fig. S4F). Taken together, our data implicated that HSPA6 transcription requires the participation of AP1 and IRF1 (Fig. 4K).

sec.title: HSPA6 negatively regulates RLR-MAVS-mediated IFN signaling
sec.p: Next, we inquired whether the induced HSPA6 influences RLR-mediated IFN signaling. Initially, we established an HSPA6-knockout (KO) cell line (Fig. 5A). Our findings revealed that MDA5-mediated IFNβ induction was enhanced in HSPA6-KO cells (Fig. 5B), throughout the process of IFNβ induction (Fig. S5A), suggesting a suppressive role of HSPA6 in the modulation of IFN signaling. In concordance, HSPA6 was also essential for the optimal induction of IFN-I by RIG-I (Fig. 5C). The ectopic expression of HSPA6 was found to suppress MDA5-mediated IFN signaling (Fig. 5D). We then delineated the critical domains of HSPA6 responsible for inhibiting IFN induction. HSPA6 possesses a DNA-binding domain (NBD) and a substrate-binding domain (SBD) [36]. The NBD, recognized as an ATPase, has its ATP-hydrolyzing activity triggered by the binding of substrate proteins via the SBD [37]. Our results indicated that the NBD is necessary for HSPA6 to inhibit MDA5-mediated IFN signaling activation (Fig. S5B). Lastly, we examined this inhibitory effect in cells infected with viruses. The expression of HSPA6 markedly reduced IFNβ induction at 24 and 36 h post-EMCV infection (Fig. 5E). Correspondingly, the EMCV RNA level increased in a time-dependent manner (Fig. 5F). Collectively, our data suggest that HSPA6 is induced by IFN-competent RLR-MAVS to attenuate IFN signaling.

sec.title: HSPA6 binds to MDA5 and impairs filament abundance
sec.p: HSPs are known to associate with misfolded proteins or protein aggregates. In the context of IFN activation, multiple copies of MDA5 molecules multimerize on dsRNAs to form filaments. We asked if HSPA6 took MDA5 multimers as their targets and affected MDA5 abundance or activities consequently. We first tested the interaction between MDA5 and HSPA6 by a co-IP assay. The anti-FLAG antibody-associated beads were used to enrich FLAG-tagged MDA5 and the co-precipitated myc-tagged HSPA6 were detected by western blotting. Data showed that WT MDA5 was able to co-precipitate HSPA6 (Fig. S5C). Interestingly, when we used anti-myc antibody-associated beads to precipitate myc-tagged HSPA6, we observed a selective binding of HSPA6 to GOF MDA5, but not to WT MDA5 (Fig. 5G). This selective binding suggested that HSPA6 recognizes filamentous MDA5 but not monomeric one. We speculated that the local concentration of MDA5 may be artificially enhanced due to the anti-Flag antibody enrichment on beads (Fig. S5C).

Next, we tested the consequence of this binding. Data showed that neither WT nor GOF MDA5 was affected at the protein level by HSPA6 overexpression (Fig. 5H and I). Then, we speculated that HSPA6 may affect the polymeric state of MDA5. We previously developed a sucrose gradient assay to measure the filamentous form of MDA5 by western blotting [38]. Using this method, we observed the GOF MDA5 distributed in sucrose fractions at higher concentrations, while WT MDA5 was almost restricted at low-density sucrose fractions (Fig. 5J). Moreover, the expression of HSPA6 dramatically pulled GOF MDA5 back into low-density sucrose fractions (Fig. 5K), indicating a negative role on MDA5 filament by HSPA6.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this study, we have unveiled that RLR-mediated IFN signaling as a new stress condition for HSPA6 expression. Our findings demonstrate that HSPA6 is specifically induced by IFN-competent RLRs, in contrast to the RLRs alone or IFNβ treatment (Figs. 1 and 2). Notably, the induction of HSPA6 is contingent upon both E3 Ub ligases and SGs, as well as the transcription factors AP1 and IRF1 (Figs. 3 and 4). The distinct kinetics of IFNβ and HSPA6 induction (Fig. 1F), coupled with the enhanced HSPA6 expression observed in IRF3 knockout conditions (Fig. 2K), suggest that HSPA6 may compete with IFNβ for access to the transcription machinery. Functionally, HSPA6 has been shown to inhibit IFNβ transcriptional activation triggered by MDA5 or RIG-I (Fig. 5). This inhibitory effect could be attributed to HSPA6’s ability to interact with the GOF form of MDA5, leading to the disruption of its multimeric status (Fig. 5).

The HSPA6 gene is mapped to the human chromosome 1, specifically at the 1q23.3 locus, and is characterized by the absence of introns. It has been documented that the HSPA6 gene lacks orthologs in rodents, such as mice and rats, but is conserved in higher mammals [39]. Thus, the study of HSPA6 in vivo is challenging. Still, evidence from cellular assays suggested that HSPA6 play roles in cellular defense. It was reported to be upregulated in response to viral infections despite the mechanisms underlying this induction and the subsequent biological implications have not been thoroughly investigated [36]. Recently, HSPA6 was identified to attenuate IFNβ induction in porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus (PRRSV)-infected cells by disrupting the interactions between TRAF3 (TNF-receptor-associated factor 3) and IKKε (inhibitor of nuclear factor kappa-B kinase subunit epsilon) [40]. Studies in other sceneries suggested that, similar to several other HSPs, HSPA6 participates in the processes of tumorigenesis and cancer progression, and is considered a potential biomarker for gastric cancer [36, 41]. Our study has identified an additional stress condition associated with HSPA6.

The membrane-less SGs in the cytoplasm play a complex role in RLR-mediated IFN activation. In the case of influenza A virus (IAV) or Newcastle disease virus (NDV) infection, for example, RLR accumulation in SGs is required for optimal IFN-I gene induction [42]. The modulating effect of SGs to absorb dsRNA stress at early time points is also reported [25]. Noted that HSPA6 is induced at a significantly slower rate compared to IFNβ upon RLR activation, our data obtained at 24 h was in line with all these observations.

Regarding the biological implications of HSPA6 expression, our study detected an inhibitory effect on IFN activation (Fig. 5). Our findings further implicated that the interaction between MDA5 and HSPA6 results in the disruption of the MDA5 multimers (Fig. 5J). While the sucrose gradient assay suggested HSPA6-mediated disassembly of MDA5 filaments, definitive visual confirmation awaits electron microscopy studies in the future to directly observe the filament state in the presence of HSPA6. A similar phenomenon has been documented with HSP40, which interacts with MDA5 and dismantles the MDA5 complex [31]. Given that HSPs are known to dissolve misfolded proteins or protein aggregates to facilitate their refolding, we hypothesized that HSPA6 may target functional RLR filaments with the aim of dissolving them.

In a preceding study, we employed a GOF mutant to investigate the impact of short peptides on MDA5-mediated IFN signaling [11]. Such GOF mutants serve as valuable tools for dissecting IFN signaling pathways without perturbing overall cellular homeostasis. Stimulation with poly I: C not only triggers the activation of wild-type MDA5 but also engages PKR and OAS, leading to a comprehensive shutdown of protein synthesis and RNA degradation [25]. Our current work further suggests that GOF mutants of RLRs could be instrumental in elucidating the regulatory mechanisms of IFN signaling.

sec.title: Cells and reagents
sec.p: HEK293, HEK293T cells and HeLa cells were cultured in Dulbecco’s modified Eagle medium (DMEM) (Gibco, 10569-010) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) (Gibco, 10099141), and 1% penicillin/streptomycin (Solarbio, P1400) at 37℃ in a 5% CO2 humidified atmosphere.

The recombinant human IFNβ (Sino Biological, 10704-HNAS) was dissolved in PBS at a stock concentration of 1.0 mg/ml as the manufacture’s instruction suggested. EGCG (TargetMol, 989-51-5) was dissolved in DMSO at a stock concentration of 10 mM.

sec.title: Plasmids
sec.p: Plasmids expressing MDA5, RIG-I, cGAS, STING, IFNβ-reporter, and the Renilla luciferase were previously described [43, 44]. Plasmid expressing MAVS [45] was kindly provided by Dr. Chengjiang Gao from Shandong University, Jinan, China. The HSPA6 CDS was synthesized and subcloned into pcDNA4/TO/myc-HisB vector by Genecreate (Wuhan, China). The G495R and C268F were respectively introduced into MDA5 and RIG-I sequences as GOF mutants [10, 17]. Together with other point mutations in GOF MDA5 (Fig. S3B), all were completed using PCR with primers bearing mutated sequence. Plasmids expressing HSPA6 truncations were obtained by overlapping PCR. All plasmids were sequenced for validation.
The sgRNA against target genes for KO were subcloned into pX459 vector and sequenced for validation. Oligo sequences are shown in Table S1.

sec.title: Transfection assays
sec.p: Cell transfection was performed when the confluency of cells reached 70–90%. Plasmids were transfected into cells using Lipofectamine™ 2000 reagents (ThermoFisher, 11668500) following the manufacturer’s instruction. When using the synthetic poly I: C (InvivoGen, tlrl-pic), plasmids expressing WT MDA5 were transfected 6 h before poly I: C transfection by Lipofectamine™ 2000, the medium was refreshed at the second transfection and the cells were harvested 18 h post RNA transfection.

sec.title: Virus infection
sec.p: Cells seeded in 6-well plates (106 to 107 cells per well) were infected separately with EMCV at an MOI of 0.01, SeV at a concentration of 20 hemagglutinating units (HAU)/ml, and HSV-1 at an MOI of 1 for 1 h in DMEM without FBS. Then the virus-containing culture supernatants were removed, and the infected cells were cultured in fresh growth medium containing 1% FBS until harvest at the indicated time points.

sec.title: Generation of KO cell lines
sec.p: sgRNA-encoding vectors were transfected into HEK293T cells and incubated for 48 h, followed by selection with puromycin at 2 µg/ml (Gibco, A1113803) for 3–4 days. For MAVS-KO single colonies generation, the pool was diluted at a density of 8 cells/ml and transferred to new plates for culturing. Single colonies were picked up and validated by PCR or western blotting.

For validation of KO efficiency, genomic DNA was extracted using TIANamp Genomic DNA Kit (TIANGEN, 4992254). A PCR amplicon was generated by using primers targeting flanking regions of sgRNA-targets and sent for sanger sequencing. The PCR primers for genomic DNA amplification are shown in Table S2.

sec.title: Luciferase reporter assays
sec.p: Luciferase reporter plasmids pGL3-IFNβ-luc and pRL-TK were co-transfected with a control plasmid or plasmids expressing MDA5. At 24 h post-transfection, the cells were harvested, and cell lysates were used to determine luciferase activity using a Firefly & Renilla Dual Luciferase Assay Kit (US EVERBRIGHT, F6075). The firefly luciferase activities were normalized by Renilla luciferase activities.

sec.title: RNA sequencing and data analysis
sec.p: HEK293 cells in 10-cm dish were transfected with plasmids expressing MDA5 for 24 h or treated with IFNβ at 1,000 IU for 6 h. Total RNA was extracted (Vazyme, R401-1) and subject to poly(A) selection-RNA sequencing by LC-Biotechnology (Hangzhou, China). The sequencing data was submitted to GenBank (GSE252140). The volcano plots and heatmap analysis were performed using ggplot2 package and “heatmap” package [46], respectively.

sec.title: RT-qPCR
sec.p: Total RNA was extracted from harvested cells by using RNA simple Total primer RNA kit (TIANGEN, DP419). RNA was reverse transcribed into cDNA using the high-performance reverse transcription kit UE Iris RT mix with DNase (All-in-One) (US EVERBRIGHT, R2028S). Then the cDNAs were subject to real-time quantitative PCR by using a 2✕SYBR Green qPCR Master Mix kit (US EVERBRIGHT, S2024). The mRNA level of glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) in each sample was used for normalization. ΔΔCT was used to calculate the fold changes relative to the controls. The Primer sequences used for RT-qPCR assay were shown in Table S3.

sec.title: Western blotting
sec.p: Cells were lysed with RIPA buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl at pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl, 1% Triton X-100, 1% sodium deoxycholate, 0.1% SDS) and the lysate supernatants were subject to SDS-PAGE and detecting target proteins using Omni ECL Light chemiluminescence (EpiZyme Bio, SQ202). The antibodies used were shown in Table S4.

sec.title: Co-immunoprecipitation assay
sec.p: HEK293T cells cultured in 10-cm dish were transfected with indicated plasmids. Cells were collected and lysed with lysis buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl at pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl, 1% NP-40, 1 mM EDTA, and 10% glycerol) containing 1 mM PMSF and 1× protease inhibitor mixture (Roche, 04693132001), and the lysates were immunoprecipitated using anti-Myc (Sigma, M5546), or anti-FLAG antibodies (Sigma, F1804) pre-incubated with Protein A + G agarose (Beyotime, P2012).

sec.title: Transcription factor prediction
sec.p: The sequences for promoter regions were obtained from Genome Browser (GRCh38/hg38) [13], a length of 2 kb upstream of the transcripts was used as promoter sequence for prediction using a virtual laboratory, PROMO version 3.0.2 [32, 33]. The maximum matrix dissimilarity rate was adjusted to 0.

sec.title: Sucrose gradient ultracentrifugation and acetone precipitation
sec.p: This protocol was established based on our previous publication [38]. Briefly, the HEK293T cells in 10-cm culturing dish were incubated with 1 ml of hypotonic buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl at pH 7.5, 10 mM KCl, and 5 mM MgCl2) on ice for 30 min. The lysates were then passed through a G25 needle 20 times and centrifuged at 5,000×g for 10 min at 4℃. Mixed 900 µl of supernatant with 3 ml of 72% sucrose in low-salt buffer (LSB) (50 mM Tris-HCl at pH 7.5, 25 mM KCl, and 5 mM MgCl2) and overlaid by 4 ml of 55% sucrose in LSB, followed by addition of 1.5 ml of 10% sucrose in LSB. The ultracentrifugation was performed at 38,000 ✕ rpm in a P40ST-2520 rotor (Hitachi, CP100 NX) for 14 h at 4℃. Fractions were collected for acetone precipitation. Briefly, one volume of gradient sample was mixed with four volumes of -20 ℃ precooled acetone and incubated at -20 ℃ overnight. The mixture was centrifuged at 12,000 g for 10 min at 4℃. The protein precipitation was dissolved with SDS-PAGE loading buffer for western blotting analysis.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Unless otherwise mentioned, all data were shown as means ± SD of three independent experiments. When there was only one variable, statistical significance between groups was analyzed using a one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by 2✕2 comparisons using Tukey’s test. When there were two variables, differences between groups were analyzed using a two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA). *, p < 0.05; **, p < 0.01; ***, p < 0.001. While ns stands for not significant. Statistical analysis was carried out using GraphPad Prism6 Software.
